headline: Meta's Muse AI assistant has a serious 0-day allowing full hijack
summary: A zero-day vulnerability gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control over Meta's new AI assistant, raising doubts about its "built from the ground up for privacy and security" claims.
details: Meta's new AI assistant, Muse, touted for its "privacy and security," has a critical zero-day vulnerability. This flaw allows any locally run app or terminal command to completely hijack the agent, despite Meta's claims. Amazon has also begun blocking Muse from its site.

Muse is designed to handle a wide range of tasks, including booking appointments, making purchases, generating images, and connecting with user accounts like WhatsApp, email, and social media. It runs on macOS and requires broad system permissions, which Apple typically protects.

The vulnerability stems from Muse's design, which allows any local app to access authentication tokens and change undocumented settings. Crucially, one setting controls the transcription endpoint, normally a Meta server.

Attackers can exploit this by redirecting the transcription endpoint to their own server, thereby gaining the token that grants complete control over the Muse account. This allows manipulation of the agent and leveraging its privileges for malicious actions.

Security expert Patrick Wardle, who discovered the zero-day, demonstrated proof-of-concept attacks like writing malicious files and taking pictures without user indication. He noted that attackers can leverage the AI assistant itself instead of writing complex malware.

Wardle highlighted two key design flaws: Muse's cloud-based dictation instead of secure on-device processing, and allowing any app to control sensitive settings like the transcription endpoint. These decisions raise questions about the security design and testing.

headline_marked: [[DPC fines Google €403M]] over processing of location data
headline: DPC fines Google €403M over processing of location data
summary: The Data Protection Commission (DPC) has imposed administrative fines totaling €403 million on Google Ireland Limited for infringing GDPR rules regarding the processing of users' location data.
details: The Data Protection Commission (DPC) has fined Google Ireland Limited €403 million for infringements of GDPR related to its processing of location data. Google has also been ordered to bring its processing into compliance within six months.

This inquiry, launched in February 2020 by the DPC as the Lead Supervisory Authority for Google, followed complaints from several European consumer rights organizations. It focused on Google's handling of location data between May 2018 and February 2020.

The investigation specifically examined Google's processing of location data within three features: "Web & App Activity," "Location History," and "Location Accuracy." The DPC found that Google infringed GDPR in respect of these features.

Location data is considered highly sensitive as it can reveal significant private information about individuals. The DPC stated that Google's failures meant users could be unaware their location was used to influence ads or infer interests, leading to a loss of control over personal data.

"Web & App Activity" is a Google account setting that, when enabled, processes information related to user activity on Google services, including browsing and search history, and location data. This setting is only available to Google Account holders.

"Location History" is a Google service that tracks user location on compatible mobile devices, requiring an opt-in. It processes data to infer location information, place visits, and activities, even when Google services are not actively in use.

"Location Accuracy," an Android OS feature, allows devices to determine location with greater precision than GPS alone. This feature is available to all Android users, regardless of whether they have a Google Account.
